Avodah Zarah 69b:12.hebrew: אָמַר רָבָא: זוֹנָה גּוֹיָה, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל מְסוּבִּין אֶצְלָהּ — חַמְרָא שְׁרֵי, נְהִי דְּתָקֵיף לְהוּ יִצְרָא דַעֲבֵירָה, יִצְרָא דְּיֵין נֶסֶךְ לָא תָּקֵיף לְהוּ.
Avodah Zarah 69b:12.english: Rava says: In the case of a gentile prostitute, where Jews are dining at her table, the wine at the table is permitted. Granted, the Jews' passion for the sin of prostitution overwhelms the Jews' judgment, and therefore they are with her, but the Jews' passion for wine used for a libation does not overwhelm the Jews' judgment, and the Jews will not allow the gentile prostitute to use it for a libation.

Avodah Zarah 69b:2.english: The mishna teaches similar cases, including the case of one who left a gentile in his shop, and the case of one who placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship. The Gemara explains: And it is necessary for the mishna to cite all these cases, even though they appear similar, as, had the mishna taught only the case of the gentile transporting a Jew’s barrels, one might assume that the reason there is no concern that the gentile used the wine in that case is because the gentile thinks that perhaps the owner will come and see him. But in a wagon or on a ship, one might say that the gentile can take his ship far off and do what he desires in such a way that the owner cannot see him.

Avodah Zarah 69b:3.english: And had the mishna taught only the case where the Jew placed his wine in a wagon or on a ship, one might assume that the concern there is because the gentile thinks: Perhaps the Israelite will come on a different road or stand on the bank of the river and see him. But in the case of a gentile in his shop, one might say that the gentile can hold the door closed and do whatever he desires with no concern of being seen. Therefore, the mishna teaches us that in all of these cases the same ruling applies, and there is no concern unless the Jew informed the gentile that he is going a great distance away.

Avodah Zarah 70a:1.hebrew: זוֹנָה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית וְגוֹיִם מְסוּבִּין — חַמְרָא אָסוּר, מַאי טַעְמָא? הוֹאִיל וְזִילָה עֲלַיְיהוּ, בָּתְרַיְיהוּ גְּרִירָא.
Avodah Zarah 70a:1.english: In the case of a Jewish prostitute and gentiles dining with her, the wine is forbidden. What is the reason? It is that since the Jewish prostitute is despised in the gentiles' eyes, she is subservient to the gentiles, and the gentiles use the wine for a libation without consideration for her.

Otzar La'azei Rashi, Talmud, Avodah Zara.english:
1907 / (Avodah Zarah 69b:) / Ḥalim
Solder / solder / to solder, to close a hole
See above, no. 1356. It refers to a barrel that had a hole and was sealed.
✭ to solder, close up a hole

1908 / (Avodah Zarah 69b:) / Shaykha
Sospiriel / sospiriel / vent hole
Missing in printings. The intention is a small hole in the barrel stopper, which allows the wine to be smelled. The word, derived from – sospirer (now soupirer) "to sigh, to breathe deeply," exists to this day in the meaning of "small cellar window" (soupirail).
✭ an air hole, a vent

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:1.english: What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - Surely, they see them touching, as it states that they were laden with ritually pure items, and these are not sealed barrels.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:2.english: By purifying his donkey drivers: - That he immersed them, and their touch is ritually pure.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:12:1.english: About contact with another: - With another am ha'aretz who encounters him on the way and was not purified for this purpose.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69a:12:2.english: Even in the first clause: - Since he went far away, there is reason to be concerned about this.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:10:1.hebrew: פשיטא: דתנא סתם לן כוותיה, ורבא מתניתין אתא לאשמועינן.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:10:1.english: It is obvious: That the Tanna taught an unattributed statement in accordance with his opinion, and Rava came to teach us this Mishna.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:10:2.hebrew: מהו דתימא: הא בבא דהיה אוכל עמו על השולחן, סיפא דמילתיה דרבן שמעון, והוא קתני לה. והכי קתני מתניתין: רבן שמעון אומר כדי שיפתח ויגוף ותיגוב, היה אוכל עמו וכו', ולא סתמא היא. קא משמע לן רבא דסתמא היא.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:10:2.english: Lest you say: That this clause, "If he was eating with him at the table," is the end of Rabban Shimon's statement, and he taught it. And thus the Mishna teaches: Rabban Shimon says, "enough time for him to open, stop, and dry," if he was eating with him, etc., and it is not an unattributed statement. Rava teaches us that it is an unattributed statement.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:11:1.hebrew: והשתא דקבעינן הלכתא כרבן שמעון דלא חייש לשתומא: לנקיבת חור שהוא בלא טורח משום דמינכר. ולפתיחת חבית כולה נמי, דחייש לה רבן שמעון, לא קיימא לן כוותיה, דהאי זיופא דטירחא הוא. ואנן קבעינן באין מעמידין (לעיל עבודה זרה דף לא.) הלכה כרבי אליעזר דלא חייש לזיופא דחותם אחד. האידנא אמאי לא מותבינן חביות סתומות ביד עובדי כוכבים?
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:11:1.english: And now that we have established the *halakha* in accordance with Rabban Shimon, who is not concerned about a bored hole: Regarding boring a hole, which is without effort, because it is noticeable. And regarding opening the entire barrel, which Rabban Shimon is concerned about, we do not maintain the *halakha* in accordance with him, because that forgery involves effort. And we established in *Ein Ma'amidin* (above, Avodah Zarah page 31a) that the *halakha* is in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who is not concerned about the forgery of a single seal. Nowadays, why do we not place sealed barrels in the possession of gentiles?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:11:2.hebrew: משום שייכא: נקב דק מאד שהוא במגופת חבית להיות ריח היין יוצא, ויש לחוש שמא יקדח שם במקצת ויטעום מן היין.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:11:2.english: Because of the bunghole: A very thin hole that is in the barrel stopper, for the scent of the wine to escape. And there is concern that he might widen it a little there and taste some of the wine.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:1:1.english: When he comes to them by a roundabout way: - When the owner can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile is afraid, thinking: 'Now he will come!'

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:2:1.english: As, had it taught a gentile - A gentile who was transporting barrels of wine:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:2:2.english: And do what he desires - And even if the owner did not inform the gentile that he was going far off, the wine would be forbidden:

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:4:1.hebrew: מחלוקת בשל סיד: במגופה של סיד שהיא לבנה, הוא דחיישי רבנן לשתומא, דכיון דלבן הוא, לא מינכר בין חדש לישן.אבל של טיט — שהוא שחור בתחלתו, ואף על פי שהוא נגוב, אינו מלבין עד יום או יומיים. דברי הכל לא חיישינן לשתומא, דמינכרא שתימת החור כשאר המגופה, ואינו אסור עד שישהא כדי שיפתח ויגוף מגופה חדשה ותנגוב.והלא שתומו ניכר: אם היה נוקב חור, הרי הוא ניכר.בין מלמעלה: שזה חדש והמגופה ישנה.בין מלמטה: כשיפתח ישראל את המגופה, יראה מתחתיה אותה סתימה, לפי שלמעלה מירח העובד כוכבים והשווה סתומו, אבל למטה לא יכול למרח וניכר.אלא אי אמרת בשל סיד: קאמרי רבנן, הא לא ידיע שתומו מלמעלה, והיכי קתני בין מלמעלה בין מלמטה?דחלים: מתמלא הנקב מלמטה כלמעלה. חלים סלדי"ר בלע"ז.פשיטא: דתנא סתם לן כוותיה, ורבא מתניתין אתא לאשמועינן.מהו דתימא: הא בבא דהיה אוכל עמו על השולחן, סיפא דמילתיה דרבן שמעון, והוא קתני לה. והכי קתני מתניתין: רבן שמעון אומר כדי שיפתח ויגוף ותיגוב, היה אוכל עמו וכו', ולא סתמא היא. קא משמע לן רבא דסתמא היא.והשתא דקבעינן הלכתא כרבן שמעון דלא חייש לשתומא: לנקיבת חור שהוא בלא טורח משום דמינכר. ולפתיחת חבית כולה נמי, דחייש לה רבן שמעון, לא קיימא לן כוותיה, דהאי זיופא דטירחא הוא. ואנן קבעינן באין מעמידין (לעיל עבודה זרה דף לא.) הלכה כרבי אליעזר דלא חייש לזיופא דחותם אחד. האידנא אמאי לא מותבינן חביות סתומות ביד עובדי כוכבים?משום שייכא: נקב דק מאד שהוא במגופת חבית להיות ריח היין יוצא, ויש לחוש שמא יקדח שם במקצת ויטעום מן היין.יצרא דיין נסך לא תקיף להו: לנסוכי.בתרייהו גרירא: דשבקה להו לנסוכי.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:4:1.english: The dispute is with regard to lime plaster: It is concerning a stopper made of lime plaster, which is white, that the Rabbis are concerned about a hole being made and sealed, because since it is white, it is not discernible between new and old.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:4:2.hebrew: אבל של טיט: שהוא שחור בתחלתו, ואף על פי שהוא נגוב, אינו מלבין עד יום או יומיים. דברי הכל לא חיישינן לשתומא, דמינכרא שתימת החור כשאר המגופה, ואינו אסור עד שישהא כדי שיפתח ויגוף מגופה חדשה ותנגוב.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:4:2.english: But with regard to clay: Which is black at first, and even if it dries, it does not whiten for a day or two. Everyone agrees that we are not concerned about a hole being made and sealed, because the sealing of the hole is noticeable compared to the rest of the stopper, and the wine is not forbidden unless there was enough time for the gentile to open the barrel, stop it with a new stopper, and for it to dry.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:1.hebrew: והלא שתומו ניכר: אם היה נוקב חור, הרי הוא ניכר.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:1.english: But isn't its sealing noticeable: If he were to bore a hole, it would be noticeable.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:2.hebrew: בין מלמעלה: שזה חדש והמגופה ישנה.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:2.english: Both from above: Because this [the patch] is new, and the stopper is old.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:3.hebrew: בין מלמטה: כשיפתח ישראל את המגופה, יראה מתחתיה אותה סתימה, לפי שלמעלה מירח העובד כוכבים והשווה סתומו, אבל למטה לא יכול למרח וניכר.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:5:3.english: Both from below: When the Israelite opens the stopper, he will see that sealing underneath it, because from above, the gentile smoothed it out and made its sealing even, but from below, he could not smooth it out, and it is noticeable.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:6:1.hebrew: אלא אי אמרת בשל סיד: קאמרי רבנן, הא לא ידיע שתומו מלמעלה, והיכי קתני בין מלמעלה בין מלמטה?
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:6:1.english: But if you say with regard to lime plaster: The Rabbis say, its sealing is not noticeable from above. So how can it teach 'both from above and from below'?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:7:1.hebrew: דחלים: מתמלא הנקב מלמטה כלמעלה. חלים סלדי"ר בלע"ז.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 69b:7:1.english: It seals firmly: The hole fills up from below as it does from above. *Ḥalim* means 'solder' in Old French.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 70a:1:1.hebrew: יצרא דיין נסך לא תקיף להו: לנסוכי.
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 70a:1:1.english: The passion for wine for a libation does not overwhelm them: To pour a libation.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 70a:1:2.english: She is subjugated to them: That she allows them to pour libations.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 129:1.english:
Wine left in a place where a gentile is present and an Israelite enters at any moment
Wine is permitted, even if an Israelite left a gentile alone in the place where the liquid is located, whether in a store, on a ship, or in a wagon; the Israelite may even be absent to go to the synagogue or any house. The same applies when a gentile transported a barrel of wine from one place to another during the absence of the Israelite, who left the gentile alone where the wine was.
GLOSE: It is forbidden to deliberately place wine or vinegar in the house of a gentile who lives alone; but when it is an accomplished fact, the wine is permitted. The wine is also permitted when the transport occurred during the absence of the Israelite who had entrusted its keeping to a gentile, for the latter fears the sudden arrival of the Israelite. In all cases, one must be unaware of what the gentile may have done, i.e., whether he closed the door or moved the wagon or ship away to evade observation.
The wine is also permitted, even if the gentile closed the store door, if it has a crack or a hole allowing one to see everything that happens inside; this case is assimilated to that of an open door. The wine is permitted only if there is a roundabout way that allows the Israelite to return suddenly, without the gentile being able to see him; the same applies when the Israelite went to the bathhouse. When the Israelite entered a bathhouse, with the gentile's knowledge, who then knows perfectly well that the Israelite will be absent for a long time; or when the Israelite told the gentile: «Guard the wine in my store well,» for the gentile then understood that the Israelite was to go away; or again when he told the gentile: «Transport the barrel of wine to such a place, I will return afterwards»; when the Israelite announced to the gentile that he was separating from him, all barrels of wine are forbidden if they are open; if they are sealed, and if the Israelite has gone far enough to give the gentile time to open and close them with clay or lime and make any trace of moisture disappear, they are all forbidden.
GLOSE: Some authors claim that wine contained in closed and sealed barrels is always permitted, because one seal is sufficient for a barrel of wine; this opinion can be admitted when the loss caused by the prohibition would be significant.

Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 129:14.english: When a gentile prostitute enters a place belonging to an Israelite and containing wine, this wine is permitted, because the gentiles would not allow such a woman to offer wine to idols; but when an Israelite courtesan, who is among gentiles, enters an Israelite's place and touches the wine there, this wine is forbidden.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: The Rishonim found this difficult: Ostensibly, from the continuation of the passage — "But if the Jew notified him that he was going far away" — it implies that as long as the Jew did not notify the gentile, the wine is considered supervised. So what is the place for this question? From Rashi's words, it appears that the question is in a case where the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away, to what extent can we consider the gentile's lack of knowledge as a reliable factor. Indeed, Tosafot explained that precisely from the precise wording of the continuation, "if the Jew notified him that he was going far away," it implies that these barrels have a special presumption of supervision, in addition to the fact that the Jew did not notify the gentile that he was going far away. The conclusion of the matter, according to the discussion in the Baraita, is that the Jew can come by a roundabout way, so that the gentile fears that the Jew might arrive at any moment (Tosafot). The Ramban has a different interpretation regarding this matter; he explains that our Mishna permitted in this case where the Jew did not notify the gentile, even with open barrels. And regarding this, the Gemara asks: How can it be said that wine is presumed to be supervised, such that the gentile does not touch it, when the gentile is carrying an open barrel of wine and the Jew does not see him? Surely the gentile can see the Jew approaching and remove his hand! To this, the answer was that there can be a presumption of supervision — by a roundabout way, where the gentile cannot see the Jew arriving.

Rashi explains: Since this is not discussing sealed barrels as in our Mishna, but rather ritually pure items (which, according to his understanding, refers to someone carrying fruits and the like), they immediately become impure through the donkey drivers, even if the owner did not notify them that he was going far away. And the Ritv'a wrote that according to Rashi's words, the question should not be understood literally, but rather in the sense: What is the reason it is permitted in the first clause? Surely it is clear that these pure items become impure. But Tosafot explained that this is not discussing fruits, but rather open barrels that contained ritually pure items. And for this reason, it is not sufficient in this case for the owner to notify them that he is going far away, as in our Mishna which deals with sealed barrels. Therefore, as soon as they are out of the owner's sight, they are forbidden, even if there was not enough time for the gentile to bore a hole, etc.

Barrels of wine that were left with a gentile are permitted if there is a roundabout way that the owner can come upon the gentile without the gentile being seen in advance, in accordance with the statement of Rava. The Rashba rules that this applies when the gentile is alone, but if there are two or more gentiles the wine is forbidden, as one of them can be on the lookout while the other tampers with the wine (Shulĥan Arukh, Yoreh De’a 129:1–2).

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were amei ha’aretz and were laden with ritually pure items and were walking in front of the owner, even if they went more than a mil ahead of the owner — these items are pure, because they are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and the donkey drivers and laborers are afraid to touch them, saying: The owner will come now, he is right behind us. This refers, according to Rava, to a case where the owner can go by a roundabout way, so that the donkey drivers and laborers do not know when the owner will come (Kesef Mishneh). But if the owner said to them: Go, and I will come after you, then once they are out of the owner's sight, the items are impure (Rambam, Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5).

Steinsaltz comment #3 on Avodah Zarah 69.english: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers were unreliable with regard to ritual impurity [amei ha’aretz] and they were laden with wine or produce that was pure, and they were walking in front of the owner, even if they moved more than one mil ahead of the owner, the items are still considered pure. This is because the workers are presumed to be under the owner's supervision, and they are afraid to touch the wine or produce, thinking the owner will come upon them at any moment. This applies where the road is a roundabout one, such that they cannot know when the owner will come upon them. If the owner said to them: Go ahead and I will come behind you, the moment they are out of the owner's sight the items are rendered impure (Rambam Sefer Tahara, Hilkhot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 13:5 and Kesef Mishne there).

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:10.english: In the explanation of the Mishna, they clarify: What are the circumstances [how exactly is it] of "under the presumption of being supervised"? And they explain: As it is taught [as it is stated in a Baraita]: If one’s donkey drivers and laborers, who were amei ha’aretz and presumed to be ritually impure, were laden with ritually pure items (wine or produce that was prepared in ritual purity), and he warns them not to touch them, but he does not know if they did so or not, even if he went away from them more than a mil — his pure items are pure, as we say that since he warned them, they are afraid of him. But if he said to them: "Go and I will come after you," so that they knew he was not going with them, then once he is out of their sight and no longer sees them — his pure items are impure.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:11.english: And they ask: What is different in the first clause [how is the beginning, in the first case, different] that if the owner went far away — his pure items are pure, and what is different in the latter clause [and how is the end different] that after the owner's eyes were out of sight — the items are impure? Rav Yitzḥak said: The first clause [at the beginning] discusses a case where the owner purified his donkey drivers and laborers for this, meaning that the owner ensured they immersed, so that they would not render the pure items impure, and therefore there is no concern about their touch.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69a:12.english: And they ask: If that is so, in the latter clause also, since the owner purified them for this purpose, why should we be concerned that they rendered the items impure? And they answer: An am ha’aretz is not punctilious about contact with another am ha'aretz. Even though they themselves were ritually pure, perhaps they encountered another am ha’aretz on the way, and the pure items were rendered impure by him, and they are not punctilious about this. And they ask: If that is so, if you are concerned about this, then let us say so even in the first clause!

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69b:1.english: When the owner comes to them by a roundabout way (winding), meaning the owner can come by a crooked, circuitous path, in a way that the donkey drivers and laborers cannot know from where the owner is coming, and therefore they are afraid. And they respond: If that is so, [if such a case is being discussed], then in the latter clause also, why should it not be said that they are afraid? And they respond: Since the owner said to them: "Go and I will come after you," their minds are at ease that the owner will not surprise them.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69b:12.english: Rava says: In the case of a gentile prostitute, where Jews are dining with her — the wine found there is permitted. Granted, their inclination for the sin of prostitution is strong for them, and therefore they are with her, but the inclination for wine used for a libation is not strong for them, and they will not allow the gentile prostitute to pour a libation.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69b:2.english: We learned in the Mishna several similar rulings: One who leaves a gentile in his shop, etc. One who places his wine in a wagon or on a ship, etc. And they comment: And it is necessary [and this Mishna needed] to state all the cases described in it, even though they seemingly are all similar in content, as, had [if it had taught] only the case of a gentile transporting barrels, we would say: There is no concern there, because [the gentile] thinks: Perhaps the owner will come and see him. But in a wagon or on a ship—[say] that he can take his ship far off and do what he desires in a way that the Israelite cannot see him.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 69b:3.english: And had [if it had taught] **in a wagon or on a ship,** we would say: There, the gentile is concerned **because he thinks: Perhaps the Israelite will come on a different road or stand on the bank of the river and see him.** But in the case of **a gentile in his shop,** [say] that **he can hold,** close, **the door and do whatever he desires** and is not concerned that he might be seen. **It teaches us** that in all cases the ruling is the same, and there is no concern unless the owner informed the gentile that he is going far off.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 70a:1.english: But if there was a Jewish prostitute and gentiles dining with her — the wine is forbidden. What is the reason? Since she is despised in their eyes, she is subservient to them, and they use the wine for a libation as they wish without considering her.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:10:1.english: What are the circumstances described by the phrase: Under the presumption of being supervised? As it is taught: If one’s donkey drivers, etc. - This is established as a case where the owner comes to them by a roundabout way, and here too, it is a case where the owner can come by a roundabout way. And it is a wonder: What is the question, "What are the circumstances"? Surely, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them that he was going far away," it implies that the first clause is where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and that is the presumption of supervision for him! And it can be said that, on the contrary, from the latter clause which teaches, "But if he notified them, it is forbidden," it implies that if so, the first clause, which teaches "under the presumption of being supervised," means that this supervision is more significant than merely not notifying them that he was going far away. And if it means, for example, [that he did not] notify them that he was going far away, the Mishna should have been silent about the phrase "under the presumption of being supervised," and we would have learned it from the implication of the latter clause. Rather, it certainly comes to say that even if he did not notify them that he was going far away, there is reason to be concerned about the matter, since the gentile sees the Jew moving away. And know that another presumption of supervision is needed, and the Gemara asks what it is, and answers: As it is taught, etc., for example, that the owner can come upon them by a roundabout way.

Tosafot on Avodah Zarah 69a:11:1.english: What is different in the first clause and what is different in the latter clause? - This means: In the first clause, why are his pure items not impure as in the latter clause? And if you say: Let him answer that the first clause deals with a case where he did not notify them that he was going far away, and therefore it is permitted, as it is taught: If he left it under the presumption of being supervised, it is permitted, and this is when he did not notify them that he was going far away. Rashi answered that it is not similar to our Mishna, for this Baraita deals with ritually pure items, such as fruits that he holds in his hands and touches at all times. Therefore, the Gemara asks why there is no distinction. Nevertheless, it is difficult: Let us establish it as referring to barrels, and there would be no difficulty, for 'ritually pure items' can also mean items in barrels. Furthermore, it is difficult: If it deals, as Rashi explained, then the Gemara should not have asked from the first clause to the latter clause, but rather should have asked directly from the first clause itself: What is the reason that in the first clause his pure items are pure, since he holds them and touches them, as Rashi explained? Therefore, it seems to Rabbi Yitzchak that it always deals with barrels, but with open ones that are easy to touch. For this reason, he cannot answer by saying that he did not notify them that he was going far away; nevertheless, it should be forbidden, and it is not similar to our Mishna, which permits wine when he did not notify them that he was going far away, for our Mishna deals with sealed barrels. And if you say: Let us still establish it as referring to sealed barrels, like our Mishna, and there would be no difficulty between the first and latter clauses. It can be said that the Baraita cannot be established as referring to sealed barrels, because it teaches: Once they are out of his sight, his pure items are impure. But if it were sealed barrels, we would require enough time for him to bore a hole, seal it, and for the seal to dry, even if he notified them that he was going far away, as our Mishna teaches.
